Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (the "RPD"), in the refugee protection claim of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the "claimant").
The claimant seeks protection, pursuant to sections 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1 IDENTITY

The claimant's identity and status as a national of Colombia is demonstrated by his testimony and a number of documents filed in evidence, including the claimant's passport, student card, Colombian personal identity card, his United States (U.S.) and Canadian visas, National Registry of Civil Status certificate, birth certificate, and various student materials.2 DETERMINATION

I find the claimant is not a Convention refugee, as I am not satisfied that he has a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in Colombia. I also find that the claimant is not a person in need of protection, in that his returning to Colombia would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and because there are no substantial grounds to believe that he would be subjected to a danger of torture in Colombia. My findings are based upon the availability to the claimant of adequate state protection in Colombia.

The claimant alleges that that he has and would continue to face persecution and a risk to his life and a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment by the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias ("FARC") if he were to return to Colombia.

The claimant's evidence is that he actively campaigned against FARC while attending university as XXXXX student, beginning in early 2006. The claimant's student activities and his opposition to the FARC are well documented in the evidence, which includes student programs and materials that name the claimant as a university XXXXX and activist opposing FARC infiltration of Colombian universities.3 I have little reason to disbelieve the claimant's evidence that he took an active XXXXX XXXXX against the FARC, leading them to pursue and persecute him.

The FARC began pursuing the claimant in XXXXX 2006 when two FARC members approached him at the university and warned him that unless he stopped his campaign, they would kill him as an example to others.

The claimant sought safety in XXXXX with the assistance of his father, who arranged for the claimant to remain in hiding with his father's friend. The claimant, as well as others in the neighbourhood noted that unknown, suspicious vehicles were parked nearby and neighbours were being asked about who lived in the house the claimant was staying in. As a result, the claimant felt threatened and moved to XXXXX to stay with a cousin in XXXXX 2007.

In XXXXX 2007, the claimant was shot at by a FARC member on a motorcycle as he was driving away from his cousin's house. The claimant was not harmed, but indicates in the narrative of his Personal Information Form ("PIF") that he had never felt such fear in his life. It was clear to him at that point that FARC was after him, and he reported the incident to the police. The "judicial police report" and the claimant's police declaration regarding the incident were provided in evidence.4

The claimant called his father from the police station and they made arrangements for him to flee to the U.S. for safety. The claimant remained in the U.S. from XXXXX 2007 until XXXXX, 2007, where he stayed with distant relatives. The arrangements kept the claimant safe, but the claimant encountered difficulties in the U.S. He found it difficult to live in the U.S. The claimant testified that his time in the U.S. was the worst" and that he did not have emotional support and felt alone. He was miserable, and convinced his father to allow him to return to Colombia - with formidable arrangements for state protection.

The claimant's father was a former director in and had held XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX For some ten years of his twenty year XXXXX XXXXX, the claimant was discretely involved with the gathering of information and intelligence to prosecute FARC. The claimant provided extensive documentation and photographs corroborating his father's involvement with XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.5 The claimant's father has strong relationships with Colombian XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, as evidenced by the arrangements he was able to make for protection of his son.

The claimant returned to Colombia from the U.S. at the end of XXXXX, 2007. His father had arranged XXXXX protection upon his arrival through a former colleague. This protection included a bullet proof Sport Utility Vehicle ("SUV"), an armed driver, and two bodyguards on a motorcycle who would accompany him at the university. The bodyguards did not stay with the claimant at all times, but the claimant testified that 24 hour protection would be provided if needed. He was told he did not have to worry. Part of the claimant's protection involved changing his location every night - sleeping in one of three different houses and moving under the cover of night.

The degree of protection provided to the claimant was both impressive and stifling. The claimant testified that in order for the FARC to get into his condominium "they would have needed a tank". He also testified that FARC does not have tanks.

In exchange for this protection, the claimant was required to provide the names of FARC informants to XXXXX from his university activities. He believes his disclosure of this information led the FARC to increase their efforts to kill him.

The claimant eventually felt that he could not continue moving around constantly with bodyguards and felt the situation was too tense and dangerous. He was also uncomfortable about the risks he was putting other people through. So the claimant decided that it would be best to leave the country once and for all. He wanted to finish the semester and enjoy a last holiday season with his family before leaving the country early in the New Year. He applied for a Canadian visa in XXXXX, which he received in early XXXXX 2007.

On the night of XXXXX, 2007, the claimant was waiting for his bodyguards to pick him up and take him to another house for the night. He saw that the street was empty and decided to venture out to the front lawn - he was immediately abducted by four armed FARC members. The claimant was forced at gunpoint into a vehicle and driven toward the outskirts of the city. During this time the claimant was threatened and beaten in the back seat. Twice they pulled the triggers on a revolver pointed at his head with one bullet in the chamber in a form of Russian roulette. The claimant was tied up with his own belt and his captors repeatedly asphyxiated the claimant with a plastic bag. The claimant tried to convince his captors that they had the wrong man, but that was unsuccessful as they replied that he should stop acting stupid because they knew he was the son of his father, who had been pursuing the FARC. Throughout this period, the claimant was questioned about the names of people who had provided information to him and his reasons for his campaign against the FARC. In an unusual stroke of luck, the vehicle approached a police checkpoint on the road to XXXXX. The abductors debated whether to shoot the claimant, but decided not to do so because they were too close to the checkpoint and feared the shot would be detected by the police. The driver ordered the claimant to be released, and he fled.

After the XXXXX incident, the claimant hastened his plans for leaving the country. He made a statement about the attack to XXXXX the next day and then stayed secure at his house until XXXXX when he was escorted by his family and bodyguards to the airport. The claimant arrived in Calgary the same day, and filed his refugee claim early in early January, 2008.

The determinative issue in this case is the availability of state protection to the claimant in Colombia. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that adequate state protection is available to the claimant if he were to return to his country.

The Supreme Court of Canada stated in Ward6 that except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown, states must be presumed capable of protecting their citizens. This presumption can be rebutted by "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect.

The initial threats and incidents that put the claimant at risk at the hands of the FARC arose in 2006 and the first half of 2007 when the claimant had little or no state protection. After the claimant's return from the United States in XXXXX 2007, the claimant received formidable state protection. The fact that this protection was adequate is demonstrated by the fact that the only peril that the claimant faced during the time he received protection arose when the claimant chose to go out on his own without protection on XXXXX, 2007. Had the claimant not ventured out of his home alone at night without protection, I seriously doubt that he would have been abducted and almost killed.

The narrative of the claimant's PIF indicates that his father is in hiding, and although there is contradictory evidence regarding whether he continues to live in Colombia,7 he remains well known and connected with Colombian intelligence and security forces and could very likely help his son obtain state protection. Upon questioning about whether the claimant could again avail himself of state protection, his response was that the problem was not whether he would get protection, but whether it would work. He subsequently stated "I suppose, yes, but I can't say for sure" when asked whether he would again receive state protection if he returned. In light of this evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the claimant could, probably with his father's assistance, again arrange state protection for his return to Colombia.

Although I can sympathize with the claimant's complaints about the intrusive nature of the security that is necessary to provide him with adequate protection, it should be recognized that the claimant is exceedingly fortunate that he has that option - without it he would likely have been killed. Moreover the adequacy of the state protection available to the claimant is the issue to be analyzed, not its objective reasonableness or the quality of life it affords. In the claimant's unique circumstances, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that adequate state protection is available if he were to return to Colombia, and he has not rebutted the presumption that the state is capable of protecting him.

Based on the aforementioned analysis, I find that adequate state protection is available to the claimant in Colombia, and as such, he does not face a serious possibility of persecution pursuant to section 96 and is not a person in need of protection pursuant to subsection 97(1) of the Act.

Accordingly, the refugee protection claim of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX is rejected. (signed) "Darcy M.
